# Cloning a Laravel Project: Resolving the Missing Vendor Directory

When you clone a Laravel project from GitHub, encountering a `Fatal error` regarding a missing `vendor/autoload.php` file is almost inevitable if you haven't prepared the repository correctly. The error message you are seeing indicates that the `vendor` directory does not exist in your local clone. This happens because Composer packages are never committed to Git by default; they occupy significant disk space and can lead to version conflicts between different environments.

The standard solution is running `composer install` immediately after cloning. However, relying on this manual step every time you pull code from GitHub introduces friction into your workflow. It breaks the seamless transition from development to production, forcing you to execute commands before verifying the application state. To eliminate this error permanently, you must configure your repository so that dependencies are managed explicitly during the build process rather than left as an afterthought.

The primary mechanism for preventing this error is ensuring the `composer.json` file and the `composer.lock` file are committed to your Git repository. The `composer.json` defines your project's requirements, but without `composer.lock`, Composer will attempt to resolve dependencies from scratch every time you run `install`. In a team environment or when deploying to production, this can result in different versions of packages being installed on different servers, leading to subtle bugs that are hard to reproduce. Committing `composer.lock` ensures that every developer and every deployment server uses the exact same set of dependency versions.

When configuring TortoiseGit or any other version control client, verify that both files are included in your `.gitignore`. By default, Laravel's `.gitignore` file includes the `vendor/` directory, which is correct behavior. You do not want to push the actual vendor folder to GitHub. Instead, you want to push the lock file. If you accidentally commit the entire `vendor` directory, it will bloat your repository size and defeat the purpose of using Composer for dependency management.

To automate this process so you never face the error again, consider adjusting your workflow slightly. When you pull changes in TortoiseGit, ensure that you are not overwriting a local `vendor` folder if one exists, but more importantly, ensure your post-clone scripts handle dependencies. While some hosting providers run Composer automatically upon deployment, local development requires manual intervention unless scripted.

You can create a simple Git hook to automate this. By creating a file named `.git/hooks/post-checkout` or modifying your local build script, you can trigger `composer install` immediately after a successful clone or pull operation. This ensures the environment is ready for production testing without requiring manual command entry. The trade-off here is that your initial clone will take longer due to downloading packages, but subsequent pulls will be fast, and you avoid the risk of forgetting to update dependencies before deploying.

Another consideration is the use of `composer update` versus `composer install`. If your local environment has an outdated lock file compared to what is on GitHub, running `install` might fail or revert changes if not handled carefully. Always ensure your `composer.lock` is up to date in the repository before pushing it. This guarantees that the error you sawâmissing autoload filesâis resolved at the moment of cloning, rendering the application ready for production immediately.

For further details on managing Laravel deployments and ensuring consistent environments across development and production servers, resources like https://laravelcompany.com provide guidance on best practices for scaling your applications without compromising stability.
